0.0.n: Introduces a contrast with what was said before.

0.1.n: The speaker refers to herself with this neutral first-person word.

0.2.n: Links 私 to もの, showing whose things they are.

0.3.n: Refers to the items bought for the speaker.

0.4.n: Casual, emphatic version of ばかり, stressing that the items are overwhelmingly for herself.

0.5.n: Connects the noun-like phrase ending in ばっかり to explanatory んです.

0.6.n: Short for の; adds an explanatory tone before です.

0.8.n: Softens the statement and leaves it open for the next thought.

1.0.n: The たら form of 気づく means when I noticed, describing a realization after something had already happened.

1.1.n: Emphasizes the surprising quantity of snacks.

1.2.n: Covers sweets and other snack foods; お is a conventional polite prefix here.

1.3.n: Identifies お菓子 as the object of buying.

1.4.n: Describes the quantity bought, reinforcing こんなに.

1.5.n: 買っちゃう contracts 買ってしまう, suggesting unintended excess; ていて describes the resulting situation and connects onward.

2.0.n: With に, acknowledges that this amount exceeds what the speaker can reasonably manage.

2.1.n: Completes さすがに; the two parts work together as one expression.

2.2.n: Names the speaker as the person who would be eating.

2.3.n: Limits the eater to the speaker, excluding everyone else.

2.4.n: Casual contraction of では; frames eating alone as the situation being considered.

2.5.n: 食べる plus きる means finish eating everything; きれない expresses inability to do so.

2.6.n: Introduces the reason for the plan that follows.

3.0.n: Used for the speaker’s own younger brother; this is a family term, not a name.

3.1.n: Lists the younger brother as one example rather than giving an exhaustive list.

3.3.n: Following 家族, specifies all the family members.

3.4.n: Marks the people who will do the eating in the てもらう construction.

3.5.n: 食べて plus もらおう expresses an intention to have others eat, treating their action as helpful to the speaker.

3.6.n: Marks the preceding intention as the content of 思います.

3.7.n: Polite form of 思う; after a form like もらおう, it expresses the speaker’s plan.

0.lit: But they are almost all my things, though,
0.tip: なんです adds an explanatory tone, while けど softens the statement and leads into more.

1.lit: When I noticed, I had ended up buying this many snacks, a lot, and,
1.tip: 気づいたら often means before I knew it, introducing a surprising situation already reached.

2.lit: As might be expected, with just me, I cannot eat everything, so,
2.tip: Adding きる to a verb means doing it completely; きれない means being unable to finish.

3.lit: I think I will have my younger brother and everyone in the family eat them.
3.tip: A verb ending in おう followed by と思います expresses a plan or intention.
